title: The butter thief's defense
hookLine: a small boy with butter on his face makes his case
carry: lila: God comes close enough to be scolded
tomorrow: what happens when a scholar comes to teach the cowherd girls?

cards: The complaint comes from the neighbors. Butter is missing from their houses again. Pots are cracked.
There are small handprints. So the accused is brought before his mother, and the song lets us see his face, still shiny with butter. He doesn't cry or run.

He opens his mouth and begins his defense. It's one of the songs carried under the name of Surdas, and it plays like a tiny courtroom: one small boy, no lawyer, and an argument he has clearly been working on.

teach.h: MOTHER, I DIDN'T EAT THE BUTTER.
teach.b: It opens with the line the whole song hangs on. Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo. Mother, I didn't eat the butter.
Then the case, point by point.
One: at dawn you sent me off behind the cows, and I wandered the forest all day. When would I have had time? Two: look at these arms.
I'm a child. How could I reach a pot hung up high? Three: the cowherd boys have it in for me.
They smeared it on my face themselves. Then he changes tactics and gets hurt. Mother, you're too trusting, you believe whatever they say.
Maybe you think I'm somebody else's child. And the big finish: here, take back my stick and my blanket. I quit.

teach.h: YASHODA SMILED AND PULLED HIM CLOSE.
teach.b: The song ends: Surdas says, then Yashoda smiled, and pulled him close against her heart. Case closed. The Bhagavata told how the butter thief stole; Surdas adds the defense, and gives the last word to a mother's smile.
Here's the teaching under the joke.

teach.h: LILA: GOD CLOSE ENOUGH TO SCOLD.
teach.b: Hindus call Krishna's childhood his lila, his play: the Lord of everything comes small enough to be caught, scolded and hugged. Many teachers read the butter as the devotee's heart, the thing he really comes to steal.

That's why he's lovingly called Makhan Chor, the butter thief, why families offer him butter and sugar on Janmashtami, his birthday, and why teams in Maharashtra build human pyramids to break a pot of curd hung up high.

how: Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo is sung as a bhajan in homes and temples, and around Krishna's birthday, Janmashtami, children sometimes act out the butter thief's story.

Hindus sing the butter song to warn children that stealing gets punished
it ends with Yashoda's smile and a hug. they sing it as lila, God close enough to be loved.
the singer names himself in the last line
Surdas says: then Yashoda smiled, and held him close.

games.q: you're small, there's butter on your face, and your mother is waiting with the neighbors' complaint. what do you do?
o: argue: the cows at dawn, my small arms, my jealous friends.
run off to the forest until it blows over.
games.why: he argues, point by point, then gets hurt and offers to quit. and it works, though not on the evidence: Yashoda smiles and hugs him.

practice: Picture the yard: the neighbors, the cracked pot, a small boy with butter on his face making his case, and Yashoda's mouth starting to twitch.
If you pray, offer Krishna something small and sweet in your mind, the way families offer butter and sugar on his birthday, and be glad that God came close enough to be scolded.
If you don't pray, bring to mind someone who argues their way out around you, and let the smile arrive before the ruling.

wordCard.voice: Surdas. The singer who let a small boy argue his case, and gave the last line to his mother's smile.

orig.note: Hindi and Braj, in Devanagari: butter, the fresh churned kind he is accused of stealing.

carryVoice: Your line: lila, God comes close enough to be scolded. A mother's smile settled the whole case. Tomorrow: what happens when a scholar comes to teach the cowherd girls?
